findings.reason: a shared refusal resolved against a different lane either refuses an entry that will launch on an execution-capable lane or admits one that launches on a non-executing lane, and §2's sixth case would pass only on a config where the two resolutions happen to coincide; the worker needs the lane expression `queue_requests` itself uses, then that lane's settings.
findings.text: §2 says execution fit "is judged against the lane the request is queued for" and names `resolve_role` (`reckon/crew/routing.py:200`) as resolving that lane's settings, but a batch entry is queued by `queue_requests` (`reckon/crew/dispatch.py:293`) on `entry.get("backend") or config["local_backend"] or config["default_backend"]` (`dispatch.py:313`, fed the entry's `backend` by `dispatch_batch.py:568`), and `resolve_role` takes a role rather than a lane and returns whatever a role/level/capability-class overlay names — so an entry that names a backend, or a project whose config sets `local_backend`, is judged against a lane other than the one its pointer records and the admission pass drains

findings.reason: the fifth done-when case fails unless the repository is passed, so the plan's own measure forces the missing input; naming it would only save the worker a round trip.
findings.text: the shared function's inputs are named as "the same locked decisions and budget ceiling", but `gate_population_finding` (called at `reckon/crew/dispatch_plan.py:862`) also needs the repository path and `plan_dispatch` skips the check entirely when `repo is None`, so a function built from the sentence's input list alone would never produce the fifth case's refusal
